content: Isoniazid is a medication primarily used to treat active tuberculosis (TB) infections in combination with other drugs. It is also prescribed alone to prevent active TB in individuals who may be infected with the bacteria, such as those with a positive TB skin test. This antibiotic is effective only against bacterial infections and does not work for viral infections like the common cold or flu. How to Use: Isoniazid should be taken orally on an empty stomach, either one hour before or two hours after meals, as directed by your doctor. For optimal results, take the medication at evenly spaced intervals. If prescribed daily, take it at the same time each day. If on a weekly schedule, take it on the same day(s) and time each week. Continue taking the medication for the full prescribed duration, even if symptoms improve. Your doctor may also recommend taking vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) to prevent nerve-related side effects. Important Warnings: Isoniazid has been associated with rare but serious liver disease, which can be fatal. The risk is higher in individuals over 35 years old, those who consume alcohol or use illicit injectable drugs, and those with pre-existing liver conditions. Liver function tests should be conducted regularly during treatment. Patients should be informed about the signs and symptoms of hepatitis, such as fatigue, weakness, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, dark urine, or yellowing of the skin/eyes, and instructed to report these symptoms immediately. Contraindications: Isoniazid is contraindicated in patients with severe hypersensitivity reactions, including drug-induced hepatitis, previous isoniazid-associated liver injury, or severe adverse reactions such as drug fever, chills, arthritis, or acute liver disease of any cause. Precautions: Patients with a history of alcohol use, malnutrition, severe renal impairment, chronic liver disease, or a predisposition to neuropathy should use isoniazid with caution. Pregnant women, malnourished individuals, or those with neuropathic tendencies should take pyridoxine concurrently. Alcohol use, renal dysfunction, or hepatic dysfunction may affect serum levels of the drug. Isoniazid is generally safe for use during lactation, as it passes into breast milk but is unlikely to harm nursing infants. Drug Interactions: Isoniazid interacts with several medications by affecting hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. It can increase the levels or effects of drugs such as simvastatin, tacrolimus, and sufentanil, among others, potentially leading to toxicity. It may also increase serotonin levels when combined with drugs like sumatriptan or venlafaxine, raising the risk of serotonin syndrome. Additionally, isoniazid may interact with foods containing tyramine or histamine (e.g. Patients should follow dietary recommendations provided by their doctor. Side Effects: Common side effects include nausea, vomiting, and stomach upset. Rare but serious side effects include severe allergic reactions, seizures, agranulocytosis, anemia, thrombocytopenia, systemic lupus erythematosus, and severe hepatitis. Patients should seek immediate medical attention if they experience symptoms of liver damage or severe allergic reactions. Storage: Store isoniazid at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Protect the medication from freezing and discard it properly when expired or no longer needed. Overdose: In case of overdose, seek emergency medical attention immediately. In the U.S., call 911 or the Poison Control Center at 1-800-222-1222. In Canada, call 1-844-764-7669. Monitoring: Regular medical and laboratory tests, including sputum tests, kidney and liver function tests, and complete blood counts, should be performed during treatment. Patients should keep all medical and lab appointments. Pregnancy and Lactation: Isoniazid is classified as Pregnancy Category C. It should be used during pregnancy only when clearly needed. While it passes into breast milk, it is considered safe for nursing infants. Additional Information: This medication may interfere with certain lab tests, such as urine glucose tests, potentially causing false results. Patients should inform their healthcare provider about all medications and supplements they are taking to avoid potential drug interactions.
